passage: Vidya noticed the new analyst before he said a word. Pranav, transferred from Lucknow to their Kochi office, spent his first Monday lunch hour on the phone arguing with a broker, and his second one staring at a banana-leaf meal as if it might bite. On Wednesday she heard him try to tell an auto driver 'Kakkanad' three different ways. By Thursday he was snapping at the printer. Vidya didn't organise a welcome party. At lunch she pushed her tiffin across: 'Appam and stew. Mild. Try.' She wrote the Malayalam for 'how much' and 'straight ahead' on a sticky note for his monitor, and told him about a notice board at the church near her house that listed rooms without brokers. On Friday she said, 'My cousins are going to Fort Kochi on Sunday. Come.' He hesitated, then said yes. That evening he sent her a photo of the sticky note and a thumbs-up 👍

qa.q: What did Vidya write on the sticky note?
qa.a: The Malayalam for 'how much' and 'straight ahead'.

qa.q: What does Pranav snapping at the printer suggest about how he felt by Thursday?
qa.a: Small hassles with the flat, the food and the language had piled up, leaving him frustrated and short-tempered.

qa.q: Why did Vidya's small gestures help more than a welcome party might have?
qa.a: The lunch, the practical tips and the Sunday invitation each eased a real problem he faced that week, which shortens the hardest stretch.

qa.q: What might the Sunday invitation mean to Pranav?
qa.a: It may be his first chance to enjoy the city instead of fighting it, and a sign that someone here has noticed him.

grounding: Shows a local colleague noticing a newcomer's struggle with flat, food and language and offering lunch, a tip and a weekend invitation.

passage:
'You're eating dry bread again,' Rashmi said, leaning on the office pantry counter.
Jeevan looked up. 'The mess near my PG closes at nine. I get back at nine-fifteen.'
'Every day?'
'Every day. Also the landlord wants a police verification form, the office says I need local address proof first, and the PG says I need the form first.'
'Classic Pune loop.' Rashmi grinned. 'Okay. One: tomorrow, lunch with us. The canteen does thalipeeth on Wednesdays. You'll like it.'
'I can't even say it.'
'Thaa-li-peeth. Two: ask HR for the company letter. They accept that as address proof. Nobody tells new people.'
'Seriously?'
'Seriously. Three: Saturday a few of us are going up Sinhagad early. Bring proper shoes, not those office ones.'
Jeevan laughed for the first time that week. 'Why are you doing all this?'
Rashmi shrugged. 'My first month in Bengaluru, someone did it for me.'

qa.q: What does the canteen serve on Wednesdays?
qa.a: Thalipeeth.

qa.q: What is Rashmi feeling while helping Jeevan?
qa.a: Rashmi feels sympathy for Jeevan, remembering being new in Bengaluru and having someone help, and wants to pass that kindness on.

qa.q: Which of Rashmi's tips breaks the paperwork loop, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Asking HR for the company letter as address proof; one small local fact like that saves a newcomer days of stress 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan to be stuck in the paperwork loop before Rashmi steps in?
qa.a: Every door seems to need another door opened first, and, tired and hungry, Jeevan has no one to ask, so the frustration builds.

grounding: Illustrates a local colleague easing a newcomer's frustrations with food and paperwork through a lunch, a practical tip and a weekend invitation.

passage:
I'm Tanvir, and I've lived in Kolkata all my life, so I didn't really notice Usha struggling at first.

She'd joined our team from Coimbatore. In the second week I saw her at lunch staring at a plate of fish curry she hadn't touched. Another day she came in soaked, having walked twenty minutes because the auto driver didn't understand "Park Circus" the way she said it. Her flat had no water on the third floor. She said all this lightly, but her jaw was tight.

I didn't do anything grand. I took her to the South Indian mess on Lake Road, where she ate like she'd found a relative. I wrote her the names of three places the way drivers say them. And I asked her to our Saturday adda at my sister's house.

She came. She laughed at my sister's jokes. On Monday she brought me a tin of murukku.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir take Usha for lunch?
qa.a: Tanvir took her to the South Indian mess on Lake Road.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling after noticing Usha's tight jaw and soaked arrival?
qa.a: Tanvir felt concerned and a little guilty for not noticing sooner, and wanted to help in simple, practical ways.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's small steps work better than a grand welcome?
qa.a: A familiar meal, the place names written the local way and one weekend invitation solved real daily problems and gave Usha a place to belong.

qa.q: What is it like for Usha in those first weeks?
qa.a: Usha is worn down and frustrated by food, transport and water problems while trying to seem fine, so the small kindnesses bring real relief.

grounding: A local colleague notices a newcomer's struggles with flat, food and language and helps with a lunch, a tip and a weekend invitation.

passage:
Team notes, Pune office, week of 12 August. Ujjwal, team lead.

Lalremsiami (joined from Aizawl three weeks ago) is doing good work but looks tired. Observed: she eats lunch alone at her desk, usually biscuits. Twice she came in late, flustered, after the bus route changed without notice. Overheard her on the phone trying to explain her rental problem in broken Hindi and hanging up close to tears.

Action taken: On Tuesday I asked her to lunch with Kedar and me at the Maharashtrian place downstairs; told her about the office shuttle she didn't know existed, and helped her fill the form. Mentioned the northeast students' group that meets on Sundays in Viman Nagar.

Friday she was on the shuttle. At lunch she laughed when Kedar struggled with her name. She's coming to our team picnic on Saturday.

Note to self: ask new joiners about the shuttle on day one.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami usually eat at lunch?
qa.a: She usually ate biscuits at her desk.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal probably feeling after overhearing the phone call?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed concerned and moved to act, noticing how close to tears the call left her.

qa.q: Which small kindness had the biggest effect, and why?
qa.a: Telling her about the office shuttle and helping with the form, because it fixed a daily frustration and got her to work calmly.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel by the end of the week?
qa.a: She likely feels less alone and more settled, laughing at lunch and agreeing to come to the team picnic.

grounding: A supervisor observes a newcomer's struggles and offers lunch, a practical tip and a weekend invitation that ease the hardest weeks.

passage:
Thursday night

Binita, the new analyst from Kathmandu, finally told me what's been wrong. She's been here five weeks and thinks Lucknow hates her.

Her landlord took a deposit and won't fix the geyser. The mess puts sugar in the dal. She keeps getting lost in Aminabad. Today at the printer she said "It's fine" three times in a row, which means it isn't.

I thought about how I'd feel dropped somewhere new. So at lunch I shared my Ammi's tiffin, the proper spicy one. She actually closed her eyes. I told her about the shared taxis to Gomti Nagar and wrote down how to ask for them. Then I just asked: "Sunday, come for kebabs with my cousins?"

She said yes before I finished.

It cost me nothing. I don't know why I waited five weeks.

Yusuf

qa.q: How long had Binita been in Lucknow?
qa.a: She had been there five weeks.

qa.q: What does Yusuf's last line suggest about how Yusuf feels?
qa.a: It suggests Yusuf feels a little regretful for waiting so long, and glad the small help mattered so much.

qa.q: What made Yusuf's help useful, and what could come next?
qa.a: Sharing tiffin, giving a transport tip and a Sunday invitation met Binita's real needs; next, Yusuf could help with how to raise the geyser problem with the landlord.

qa.q: How might Binita feel after Yusuf's invitation?
qa.a: Binita probably feels relieved and welcomed, since she said yes before Yusuf even finished asking.

grounding: A local colleague notices a newcomer's frustrations and offers a lunch, a tip and a weekend invitation that shorten the hard weeks.

passage:
[Tuesday, 1:05 pm, office chat]
Rashmi: Raghav, saw you eating biscuits at your desk again. Third day in a row 😅
Raghav: haha. canteen menu is all in Marathi and I didn't want to point at random things
Rashmi: Fair. Come down with me, I'll order for both of us. The misal is good if you like spicy
Raghav: yes please. also sorry, one more question
Raghav: the flat broker wants 3 months' deposit and says everyone pays that. is that normal here?
Rashmi: Ask him to put it in writing, and check a couple of other listings before you agree. My cousin had the same broker trouble
Raghav: ok thanks. I'll check more listings first
Rashmi: And this Sunday a few of us are going up to Sinhagad fort. Easy walk, bhajiya at the top. Come?
Raghav: really? I've just been sitting in my room on weekends
Rashmi: Then definitely come. I'll send the pickup time 🙂
Raghav: thank you. first time this week I don't feel like an alien here

qa.q: What does Rashmi say is good at the canteen?
qa.a: Rashmi says the misal is good if you like spicy.

qa.q: What does Rashmi's first message suggest about how Rashmi feels?
qa.a: Rashmi was concerned and sympathetic after noticing Raghav eating biscuits at the desk three days in a row, and wanted to help without making it awkward.

qa.q: Which of Rashmi's small kindnesses might help Raghav most, and why?
qa.a: Ordering lunch, a simple tip to check other listings before agreeing, and the Sunday invitation each ease a daily struggle, which matters more in the hard first weeks than a big welcome.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Raghav feels relieved and less alone, saying it is the first time this week that the city doesn't feel alien.
